book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge

chapters.file: ch18 - Of Science, Sorcery, and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: The chapter reads Strange's conversion from neurosurgeon to sorcerer as a Kuhnian paradigm shift: his medical materialism is 'normal science' puzzle-solving that keeps resisting anomalies (Pangborn's impossible recovery, the astral projection, the multiverse tour) until Kamar-Taj offers a rival paradigm with its own exemplars, which he can only adopt by learning 'knowledge how' through tedious practice. It explains incommensurability through Strange's inability to rationally persuade his old medical colleagues, then contrasts Kuhn with Popper's falsificationism, Feyerabend's 'anything goes' anarchism (sorcery once looked as disreputable as early heliocentrism), and Lakatos's progressive versus degenerating research programs to ask whether sorcery could count as a science in Strange's world.

chapters.file: ch19 - We’ve Run Out of Time… or Have We.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues that the film's multiverse, where sorcerers 'harness energy drawn from other dimensions,' is best modeled on the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, walking through Tegmark's Level I-III multiverses, Schrodinger's cat, the double-slit experiment, and the measurement problem (Copenhagen, von Neumann-Wigner's mind-caused collapse, and Everett's branching) to show that interpreting the formalism is philosophy rather than physics. It defends many-worlds against the objections of counterintuition and Ockham's razor, and suggests that Strange trapping Dormammu in a time loop works like a quantum experiment, with branching worlds dissolving the grandfather paradox.

chapters.file: ch20 - Knock and the Door Will Be Opened… Eventually.md
chapters.relation: The chapter reads Strange pounding on Kamar-Taj's door as Kierkegaard's passionate collision with 'that which thought cannot think': the materialist surgeon hits the unknown as a frontier, takes offense at the Ancient One's talk of healing through belief, and can only proceed by surrendering intellectual control ('I control it by surrendering control?'). It applies Kierkegaard's two teachers from Philosophical Fragments: Pangborn is healed the Socratic way, recollecting a power already within him, while the Ancient One's astral knock-out and eviction of Strange acts like the god as teacher, forcing him to discover that he is untruth, until faith becomes 'controlling magic by surrendering to it.'

chapters.file: ch21 - Part V “IT’S NOT ABOUT YOU”.md

chapters.relation: The chapter argues Strange fails Aristotle's golden mean at both stages of his life: as a surgeon he chose cases for money and fame (greed and gluttony rather than generosity and temperance), and as Sorcerer Supreme he swings to the opposite extreme of total self-denial, refusing sleep, love, and friendship with Clea, Wong, and the Ancient One, since relationships between unequals cannot be the reciprocal philia Aristotle demands. It reads his hardest choices—the Dark Dimension left to Dormammu to save Earth, the Illuminati destroying parallel Earths during the incursions, and spending the last drop of the panacea on Wong rather than the world—as tragic dilemmas that show both the virtue ethicist's need for judgment and a defensible-but-excessive partiality toward friends.

The chapter uses Michael Walzer's Problem of Dirty Hands to weigh the Ancient One's secret lifelong use of forbidden dark magic against Kaecilius's summoning of Dormammu, arguing that only she faces a genuine dirty-hands dilemma because her end (defending Earth) is good while his is not. It asks why dark magic is forbidden at all and answers with rule-utilitarian reasoning that has taken on a deontological life of its own, then invokes Kant's murderer-at-the-door essay to argue, with Mordo's 'the bill comes due,' that whoever does wrong for good ends bears responsibility for the downstream consequences—and that Strange's willingness to break Kamar-Taj's rules while accepting the cost is what makes him a hero.

The chapter asks whether Wong's hereditary service to the Sorcerer Supreme is culpable servility, framing the charge with Kant's line that 'one who makes himself a worm cannot complain' and Thomas E. Hill's Kantian account of servility as failing to claim one's dignity as a person. It answers with Hegel's master-slave dialectic: Strange, free to haunt the astral plane, becomes dependent on Wong for everything worldly, while Wong, by working on the world rather than merely commanding it, develops the self-consciousness Hegel says work produces—he serves the shared mission rather than the master—so the relationship is a partnership in which servitude grounds rather than forfeits Wong's self-respect.

chapters.file: ch25 - By the Crimson Bands of Cyttorak… We Conclude!.md
chapters.relation: The chapter weighs Strange's choice in Doctor Strange: The Oath to spend the last drop of the panacea curing Wong's brain tumor instead of having it replicated to cure all disease, arguing it violates 'first, do no harm' and the Hippocratic precepts—not least because Strange is Wong's friend rather than his physician and invokes a no-longer-binding oath. It then argues his sorcerer's ethics fit the martial arts warrior way better: 'hurt rather than harm' from Master Kan in Kung Fu and the Pinan forms, Zen-shaped bushido's self-control, Confucian responsibility and care for society, and the Tao Te Ching's balance and thousand-mile journey as the shared ethos of medical, martial, and mystic training.

chapters.file: ch26 - Part VI “I’VE COME TO BARGAIN”.md

chapters.relation: The chapter asks whether Dormammu is truly evil and tests him against Augustine's three types of evil: metaphysical evil as privation fails because Dormammu is a positive being with a face and a voice, natural evil fails because he is a sentient agent with intentions, so he lands squarely in moral evil—freely intending to deprive intelligent beings of the good of existence. It entertains the Galactus-style alternative that Dormammu, like a lion taking a gazelle, is an amoral force consuming worlds for survival, but his rage in the time loop ('your world is mine, like all worlds') reveals a drive for domination rather than sustenance, while conceding we know him only through the Ancient One's possibly biased testimony.

The chapter pairs Strange's midlife collapse with Tolstoy's crisis in A Confession—both famous egotists who found their glittering lives 'a stupid fraud'—using Tolstoy's fable of the traveler licking honey above the dragon of death to read Strange's desperate medical questing as vain honey-licking. It lays out Tolstoy's doctrine of nonresistance: violence is forcing others against their will, every act of violent resistance multiplies evil, and the state's division of cruelty makes killing mechanical, then asks whether Tolstoy could accept Strange's metaphysical war, concluding from Tolstoy's remark that he would axe a bear to save a peasant (but not kill the highwayman) that he could endorse magical violence against Dormammu while still forbidding violence against human beings.

The chapter argues that Strange's universe implicitly contains the Creator God of theism rather than just Marvel's gods: Aristotle's impersonal prime mover will not do because Strange needs a relatable source of an objective moral order, so Aquinas's all-good author of eternal, natural, and divine law supplies the framework. It reads three comics as evidence: Strange defeating Dracula by invoking the Tetragrammaton, the Sise-Neg saga where a sorcerer who attains godhood at the dawn of time learns to recreate the universe exactly as the first cause made it, and the World War Hulk story where summoning Zom shows the hubris of violating the moral order—closing with C.S. Lewis's 'deep magic' as cooperation with the created order versus dark magic's will to control it.

holes.name: Imre Lakatos
holes.what: Philosopher of science who judged research programs progressive or degenerating by whether modifications to the 'protective belt' around a theory's 'hard core' yield novel predictions.
holes.why: Chapter 18's closing section uses Lakatos's criterion as a third alternative to Kuhn and Feyerabend for deciding whether medicine and sorcery are rationally progressive.

holes.name: Many-Worlds Interpretation and the Measurement Problem
holes.what: Everett's interpretation of quantum mechanics on which the wave function never collapses but branches at every quantum event into parallel worlds, central to the measurement problem.
holes.why: Chapter 19's whole argument is that the film's multiverse is a many-worlds multiverse, and taxonomy has no concept covering quantum-mechanics interpretations.

holes.name: The Problem of Dirty Hands
holes.what: Walzer's dilemma of the person in power who must violate moral principles to achieve a good end, leaving hands dirty even when the act is justified.
holes.why: Chapter 23 is organized around this problem, applying it to the Ancient One's dark magic, Kaecilius, and Strange's rule-breaking bargain with Dormammu.

holes.name: Thomas E. Hill Jr.
holes.what: Contemporary Kantian philosopher known for 'Servility and Self-Respect,' which condemns servility as failing to assert one's equal dignity as a person.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central question—whether Wong's lifelong service is wrongful servility—is built directly on Hill's servility and self-respect argument.

holes.name: Leo Tolstoy
holes.what: Russian novelist-thinker whose later Christian philosophy of nonresistance rejected all violence, state power, and property as sources of evil.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is built entirely around Tolstoy's Confession and his doctrine of nonviolence, yet he is absent from the taxonomy while his follower Gandhi is present.
